subjects.displayTitle: The Declaration of Baha’u’llah: a garden open to all
subjects.introduction: An order of banishment arrived in Baghdad, and Bahá’u’lláh answered it by moving to a garden. For twelve days the garden of Najíb Páshá stood open to the whole city: governor, officers, divines and notables came by day and by night, and a man under sentence of exile received them with a sovereignty that left the people of Iraq, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says, as witnesses. Within that hospitality, by hints and allusions, Bahá’u’lláh first made known that He was the One the Báb had promised; some of the friends grasped His meaning and others did not, and full understanding came later. Jesus reading Isaiah in the synagogue and declaring the words fulfilled in the hearing of those present poses the same question of how a proclamation asks its hearers to see their own moment [1]. The Riḍván declaration is told in the language of a renewed creation, gardens awakening, light spreading from East to West, old enemies made brothers, and it asks for a response in conduct as well as belief. To follow it further is to turn toward the person of Bahá’u’lláh, and then along the road of banishment to Constantinople and the life that awaited Him there.
subjects.arc: Enter through the garden’s welcome, follow the accounts of declaration and recognition, then explore fulfilment through the images and practices of a renewed world.

order.why: Distinguish the garden’s allusions from their differing reception.
shortened: Leaving the city, Baha'u'llah went to the garden of Najib Pasha and resided there for twelve days. During that time many people, both high and low, and even the Governor and a number of other officials, attained His blessed presence. These are the twelve days of Ridvan.

In any event, it was by means of hints and allusions that Baha'u'llah first declared His mission during those twelve days. Certain among the friends grasped His intent, but others did not fully understand.

order.why: Open with the garden’s welcome to all.
Read the gatherings beside the threat of exile.
shortened: Yet, although subject to banishment and exile, Baha'u'llah nevertheless moved with the utmost dominion to the garden of Najib Pasha, where for twelve days the Cause of God was exalted to such an extent that the Governor, Namiq Pasha; all the high-ranking officers of the army and the province; the country's religious dignitaries; and the nation's notables came by day and by night to attain His presence. All this, notwithstanding the fact that He was, to outward seeming, an exile! Yet the pervading influence of the Cause of God, the sublimity of His Word, and the diffusion of the divine fragrances were such that those few days were passed in intense joy and delight, and the Ridvan Festival was inaugurated.

order.why: Keep the recollected farewell visits in view.
Retain the departing community’s affection and grief.
shortened: O servant in attendance! For twelve years We associated and consorted with the people of Iraq with perfect love, harmony and favor. At the time of Our departure from the house and arrival in the garden which was named Ridvan, most of the officials and notables of the government and country were grieved to witness it, and some of the princes wept. In truth, a new resurrection arose....

order.why: Connect announcement with joy amid banishment.
Read the reported declaration and festival.
shortened: In that garden His blessed tent was raised, and in that very hour, to spite the enemies, the Festival of Ridvan was proclaimed. At such a time, during the Blessed Beauty's exile when the friends were in anguish, with supreme power in the afternoon of Ridvan, immediately upon arrival at the garden, the Festival of Ridvan was announced and the Cause was proclaimed. Outwardly, until that day there had been no mention of "Him Whom God shall make manifest" - on that day He made mention of it.

order.why: Preserve the particular recollection of the ninth day.
shortened: This was the ninth day that the Blessed Perfection leaving Bagdad, stayed in the garden of Najib Pasha before starting for Constantinople.

order.why: Describes the Ridvan garden, the twelve-day festival and its relation to the Ancient Beauty’s departure from Baghdad.
Keep the extended and polemical recollection attributed.
shortened: When they wanted to move the Blessed Beauty from Baghdad, Namiq Pasha sent the order and official papers to His presence with the message that "Once before an order came and we wrote some excuses to the Sublime Porte. This is the second time these orders have come and there is no choice but to execute them." At that time the Blessed Beauty, may His glory be exalted, accepted and preparations for departure were made. Although He never liked pomp, nevertheless He said "In these days we must depart with utmost majesty." Therefore He went to the Pasha's garden and stayed for twelve days, arranging festivities and celebrating the Most Great Festival.
But Mirza Yahya was afraid and very unstable in temperament.

order.why: Consider titles and the reported public claim.
Read the numerical interpretation without conflating its chronology with Ridvan.
shortened: Then came this blessed verse: "This is naught but a Reminder to the worlds" - that is, the one asked about is but the Great Remembrance of God, and "ye shall surely know its tidings" means what He will inform and announce "after a time" - that is, after the year sixty-eight corresponding to the numerical value of "Hin" (time), for after year sixty-eight comes year sixty-nine, and this is the year of the manifestation of the Ancient Beauty, as the Most Glorious Beauty, exalted be He, hath said: "Then in the year nine ye shall attain unto all good."

order.why: Turn from narrative to the announced Beloved.
Consider the relation of the new claim to the Bayan.
shortened: The All-Compelling One hath appeared after the Qa'im and is seated upon the throne of the Bayan.

order.why: Hear the Herald’s glad tidings.
shortened: He informed the world of the Most Great Manifestation and gave them glad tidings of this Name whereby every heedless and remote one hath lamented.

order.why: Read the claim concerning the promises of religions.
shortened: This is the Day wherein the ocean of divine knowledge hath surged before the faces of all religions, and the hidden and treasured Mystery hath been revealed, through which the Herald proclaimed: "He hath come, He at Whose mention Paradise and the Most Exalted Garden were attracted."

Say: O peoples of the earth! The All-Bountiful hath come, riding upon the clouds, while from His right the Herald of Glory proclaimeth: "O people! This is He Who was promised to you in the Books of old, and this is He at Whose appearance the Books of the peoples bowed down in submission."

order.why: Attend to the imagery of the world bearing witness.
Extend that imagery through sea, sun, and heaven.
shortened: The sea hath testified to the Most Great Sea, and the sun to this Luminous Orb. The heaven hath borne witness to the Lord of Names, and the light to this Revelation whereby the horizon of the world hath been illumined.

order.why: Consider the upheaval accompanying the advent.
shortened: Say: He hath come with the truth, and by Him the fruits have fallen from the trees, and the souls of the righteous were stirred, and the pillars of creation were shaken.

order.why: Read departure as the removal of veils.
shortened: This is the day when the Ancient Beauty moved toward another mansion, despite those who denied the Day of Judgment - the Day in which the veils were rent asunder, the clouds were dispersed, and the lights of the Countenance appeared from this luminous horizon.

order.why: Hear the invitation voiced through the Spirit.
shortened: The Beloved calls out: "The Best-Beloved has come with clear sovereignty!" And the Spirit proclaims before His face: "That which was hidden in the heaven of your Lord's will, the All-Knowing, the All-Informed, has been made manifest!"

order.why: Retain the reported account of lineage and the Bab.
Place the announcement amid religious enmity.
shortened: His Holiness Baha'Ullah appeared about sixty years ago in Persia, at a time when among the people of Persia there was strife and enmity unspeakable, to the extent that each considered the other religionists as outcasts.

order.why: Read the reported contrast between prejudice and illumination.
Keep the further account of religious conflict attributed.
Consider the reported imagery of sunrise in the East.
Read the instruction about presenting that change.
Examine the relation between inherited tradition and unifying light.
Consider the reported renewal of Christ’s teachings.
Look for the concrete sign of formerly hostile peoples uniting.
shortened: At this time, Baha'u'llah, like the sun, rose from the eastern horizon and through the lights of truth promoted teachings whereby these conflicting, quarreling, hostile peoples entered beneath the tabernacle of the oneness of the world of humanity.

order.why: Follow the movement from East to West.
shortened: Now the light of Baha'u'llah has illumined East and West and set the world of creation in motion. Despite this, is it fitting for those who consider themselves believers in the Primal Point (may my spirit be sacrificed for Him) to remain veiled from this mighty Cause?

order.why: Enter the imagery of a new morning and spirit.
shortened: Praise be to God, a world-illumining ray made the universe the court of the Sun and bestowed a new spirit upon the world of the soul. The dark night of deprivation passed and the luminous morn of effulgence dawned. The Beloved of the horizons stepped gracefully into the garden court and became the Beauty of the assembly.

order.why: Read the world imagined as a garden of unity.
shortened: O lions of the forest of divine unity! The Sun of the heaven of the Glorious Lord and the unique Light has risen from the horizon of the world with a world-illumining ray that brightened the infinite expanse of the material and spiritual realms and made the plane of contingency the envy of rose gardens and meadows.

order.why: Consider the renewal of withered hope.
Hear the celebration of creation clothed in glory.
shortened: O thou who hast succeeded in turning toward the Most Glorious Horizon!

By God the True One, all contingent being struts in robes of glory and boasts over the supreme realms throughout creation, for the Most Great Luminary, the Ancient Beauty, the Sun of Glory hath shone forth upon all regions and directions, and the earth is illumined by the light of its Lord.

order.why: Connect Ridvan’s joy with spiritual springtime.
shortened: Tear the collar of patience and raise high the melody and song of the Greatest Glad-Tidings, saying: The divine morn has dawned! The Sun of Reality has shone forth! The divine springtime has arrived and the life-giving breeze of the Kingdom has wafted! The Most Exalted Beauty appeared and the Sun of the horizon of truth became manifest and evident! He made the world a paradise of Ridvan and made the earth the envy of heaven!

order.why: Read the reported account of a new cycle and changed laws.
Return to the universal call and open doors.
End with the invitation to hear and emulate.

questions: How does the setting of impending banishment change the meaning of the garden’s welcome and joy?
What distinctions emerge between announcement, recognition, and later understanding in these accounts?
How do the images of light and springtime relate to the concrete change from enmity to fellowship?
What does Luke’s account of proclamation and fulfilment illuminate, and what remains distinct about the Ridvan accounts?
What might it mean to respond to this declaration through conduct as well as belief?

references.label: 1 · Luke 4:16–21 · Proclamation and fulfilment
references.note: Jesus reads Isaiah in the synagogue and declares its fulfilment in the hearing of those present. Compare the relationship between inherited promise, a public announcement, and the listener’s recognition. The scenes and religious claims remain distinct; the comparison opens a question about how a proclamation asks its hearers to understand the present.

subjects.displayTitle: The Ascension of Baha’u’llah: grief and continuing presence
subjects.introduction: On the night of the Ascension, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá later wrote, sorrow intensified upon Him beyond anything He had known; the once bright days turned black, and after His Father’s departure He found Himself, in His own words, all alone, with enemies within and without. And yet Bahá’u’lláh had promised, a few days earlier, to be with Him always, and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá came to say that a person holding every Tablet without that presence has nothing, while one holding not a word but living in it has everything. Grief and continuing presence sit together here without one cancelling the other, and the way through them was the Covenant, tested at once by the theft of papers and seals and by every friend who had to decide where loyalty lay. Jesus’ promise not to leave His disciples comfortless, bound as it is to keeping His commandments, offers a kindred joining of presence and fidelity [1]. The road leads on into lamentation and the expressions of grief, into the meaning of Covenant-breaking, and into the station and authority of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá.
subjects.arc: Begin with grief, approach the remembered closing days, then consider consolation, the Covenant, and the forms of service through which memory becomes active.

order.why: Keep the brief recollection of gathering papers.
Open with the lived weight of separation.
shortened: But then came the Beloved's departure from this world.
The Supreme Affliction was upon us, separation consumed us, the once bright days turned black as night, and all those roses of other hours were dust and rubble now.
This went on until the day Baha'u'llah ascended. At that supreme affliction, that shattering calamity, Nabil sobbed and trembled and cried out to Heaven.

order.why: Hear the reported loneliness in its starkest form.
shortened: After the ascent of Baha'u'llah I was all alone. Enemies within and enemies without have attacked me and thousand difficulties surrounded me.

order.why: Pause with remembrance on the night of the Ascension.
shortened: O you whom I remember on this darkest night, the night of the Ascension, when sorrows have intensified upon 'Abdu'l-Baha.

order.why: Recounts intensified opposition and burdens following Baha’u’llah’s ascension.
Allow the unrelieved intensity of mourning to be heard.
Consider how this loss enters consolation for other bereavements.
shortened: O thou who art stricken with the most great calamity! Calamities and heart-numbing losses are indeed hard to bear, inasmuch as love and affection torment the heart from the flame of separation. But when we recall the ascension of the Ancient Beauty and the heart-numbing loss of the Greatest Name, all of our other troubles will vanish, for deprivation from His sunlike face maketh separation from a shining lamp easier to bear, nay, it dispelleth it from the mind.

order.why: Read the sorrow of a seeker arriving too late.
shortened: When he set foot on the path yearning to quench his thirst from this soft-flowing river, he discovered that Thy most effulgent Beauty had ascended unto the realm on high.

order.why: Place departure within the remembered life at Bahji.
Read the recollected intimations in prayer.
Hear the account of entrusted writings and personal emotion.
shortened: A few days before the Ascension of the Blessed Beauty, may my spirit be sacrificed for His loved ones, He commanded 'Abdu'l-Baha to gather the papers in His blessed chamber and put them in a bag. According to His blessed command, the papers were collected and placed in two bags. He said "These papers are entrusted to you." When these words issued from His pure lips, the condition that arose is indescribable - all my limbs trembled and tears flowed like rain.

order.why: Compare the reported assurance accompanying that trust.
shortened: A few days before his departure Baha'u'llah called me into his bedroom and commanded me to gather together all his writing and Tablets telling me that 'they shall belong to thee'. This command agitated me and I was very sad at heart, because I understood the days of his ascension are drawing nigh.

As he looked in my face he saw my condition and said:- 'Rest thou assured! Let not thy heart be troubled. I am with thee always. My confirmation shall always reach thee.' This promise which is more than a certainty has been the cause of my consolation.

order.why: Keep the remembered warning about the Covenant attributed.
Notice the particular remembrance of the friends in Nayriz.
Read the interpretation of the Tablet of the Vision.
shortened: This is what He foretold in His holy tablets and hidden scrolls beforehand, including what was revealed in the widely known and circulated Tablet of the Vision throughout the horizons of the world: that the ascension would be from the prison of Akka - and there is no altering the words of God. He said, and His word is the truth: "Whereupon all existence cried out saying: 'May all beings be a sacrifice for Thy tribulation, O King of earth and heaven! To what end hast Thou committed Thyself to be among these people in the city of Akka? Proceed to Thine other dominions, to realms which no eyes of the people of names have ever beheld.' Thereupon We smiled."

order.why: Retain the reported epidemic as an account of events.
Distinguish the further recollection and quoted interpretation from a medical explanation.
shortened: Until His ascension occurred, there was no cholera anywhere, but then it broke out in 'Akka. All the people, especially the Christians, fled. Mikhail Khammar said that the talisman of 'Akka was broken, for after the ascension of the Blessed Beauty, diseases again prevailed in 'Akka.

order.why: Turn to the sun’s continuing light from the unseen realm.
shortened: The world's great Light, once resplendent upon all mankind, hath set, to shine everlastingly from the Abha Horizon, His Kingdom of fadeless glory, shedding splendor upon His loved ones from on high and breathing into their hearts and souls the breath of eternal life.

order.why: Consider grace as an ongoing presence.
shortened: Behold, then, before you the effulgence of the Most Exalted Friend. Although the Greatest Name hath passed on to the Invisible Realm, although the Daystar of the Ancient Beauty, may my spirit be sacrificed for the dust of His Threshold, hath set on the horizon of this contingent world, yet the bounties emanating from His presence are around us ever more and the waters of His grace are constantly poured forth.

order.why: Hear the assurance of all-embracing bounty.
Connect that assurance with gratitude.
shortened: O thou who gazest toward the divine realm! Give thanks for the hidden favors of the Blessed Beauty, that after His ascension to His mighty Kingdom, He did not deprive us of His exalted bestowals nor leave us bereft of His all-embracing bounties.

order.why: Read the reported vision and its supplied interpretation.
Consider the image of stars drawn toward the Kingdom.
shortened: Yet when the Sun of Truth ascended to the heaven of sanctification and the Most Great Luminary rose to the Kingdom of uniqueness, these brilliant stars are also attracted in their ascension to that apex of radiant stations, and these stars are drawn to the Kingdom's horizon.

order.why: Follow the movement from storm and darkness toward assistance.
Recognize the continuing tempest of trials.
shortened: After the ascension of the Beauteous Beloved, it is another tempest of trials that now rages. To seek rest and desire comfort and pursue tranquility is like searching for dry land in the Most Great Sea or seeking coolness and moisture in fire. One must have absolutely no hope for comfort, joy or security.

order.why: Keep the polemical imagery within the letter’s conflict.
Retain the situated account of changing allegiances.
shortened: While before the Ascension of the Blessed Beauty when there was no ulterior motive, no one mentioned his name and if he died no one would visit him - this servant day and night overseen his affairs and let no dust settle upon him. But after the Ascension every wavering one shows him utmost sincerity.

order.why: Consider recurring doubt after a Manifestation’s passing.
shortened: Although they had experienced during the days of His holy Manifestations that no diminution occurred in Their Cause after Their ascension, yet following the ascension of the Most Great Luminary the people of doubts and suspicions were again stirred into motion.

order.why: Read steadfastness amid grief and division.
shortened: And when the pillars of the world were shaken by the ascension of the Desired One - may my spirit be a sacrifice for His loved ones - and the most great calamity raised its banner at the center of contingent being, and all existence burst into lamentation and crying, and the sea of tests surged with utmost turbulence and tumult, they remained supremely firm and steadfast in the Covenant, resolute in the Testament, and kept their distance from the people of violation.

order.why: Connect shared sorrow with uniting the friends.
Read the reported comparison with Christ’s companions.
shortened: The Blessed Beauty hath placed upon the heads of His loved ones, particularly those who were in the Most Great Prison, the crown of eternal sovereignty. Even as in the time of Jesus the Son of Mary, those who were under the shadow of Christ knew not in what shadow they dwelt, but afterwards they proved faithful. May my soul be a sacrifice for them! Yet during His own time they achieved nothing. Now too it is not known what name the Blessed Beauty hath bestowed upon His loved ones, especially those who were in His company in prison. They bore hardships and found no rest throughout their days.

order.why: Consider the call to endurance.
Keep the demanding interpretation of trials in its setting.
Hear the urgency of continuing service.
Read the further insistence on dedication.
Give that dedication the form of active service.
Consider the portrait of lives shaped by devotion.
shortened: O true servant of the Abha Beauty! After the ascension of the Blessed Beauty, may my spirit be a sacrifice for His loved ones, holy souls forgot this world and saw themselves in the Abha Kingdom, and conducted themselves accordingly. Day and night they devoted their time to serving the Cause of God. They sought neither comfort, nor bounty, nor security, nor pleasure.
These souls are Baha'i, they are divine, they are luminous, they are of the All-Merciful. They cast no shadow, but are rather light from head to foot.

order.why: Ask how witnessing becomes responsibility to others.
Read the call to demonstrate continuing vitality.
shortened: Today is the day when we must prove and demonstrate, and make manifest and evident before the eyes of all the world, that the ascension and passing of the Sun of Truth did not cause any weakness or degradation in the Cause of God.

order.why: Consider the confidence in a widening influence.
shortened: Soon every disappointed and lost one will observe that after the ascension of the Blessed Beauty the divine lamp grew brighter and the Sun of Truth more resplendent, the waves of the Most Great Sea grew stronger and the melody from the divine gardens more widespread. The fame of God's Cause was raised throughout the horizons of the world and the might of divine power set the pillars of nations in motion.

order.why: End with gratitude expressed through virtues.

questions: How can the passages affirm continuing presence while acknowledging the depth of grief?
What changes when we read a letter, a recollection, and a reported vision alongside one another?
How does the Covenant connect personal bereavement with responsibility for the community?
What similarities and differences emerge beside John’s connection between love, presence, and keeping the commandments?
What forms of remembrance might cultivate virtues, unity, and service without silencing sorrow?

neighbors.invitation: Explore the language and experience of grief.

references.label: 1 · John 14:18–21 · Presence, love, and faithful action
references.note: Jesus promises that his disciples will not be left without comfort and relates love to keeping his commandments. Compare this conjunction of continuing presence and active fidelity with the passages on grace, virtues, and the Covenant. Attend to each text’s particular account of the relationship between the divine messenger and the community.

subjects.introduction: Thirty stages lie between Tehran and Baghdad, and on that winter road of frostbitten feet and halvah salted with pepper by mistake the exiles did not meet a single believer. Yet ‘Abdu’l-Bahá remembered the journey as full of joy because it was in the path of God, and the city it led to became a place of renewal rather than oblivion. Bahá’u’lláh would sit in the coffeehouse making strangers into friends, come back from two years alone in the Kurdish mountains wearing a coarse sleeveless jacket, and fling open the doors to the learned of every people. A few believers crowded into one small room sang all night so that comfortable neighbours envied them. Jeremiah told the captives in Babylon to build houses, plant gardens and seek the peace of the city, and that counsel to make a home of exile is a fit companion to these years [1]. From here the story opens into the withdrawal to Sulaymáníyyih, the early ministry of Bahá’u’lláh, and the chain of banishments that carried Him on to the sea.
subjects.arc: Begin with hospitality, trace arrival and separation, then follow renewed teaching and the everyday acts through which a community found joy and purpose.

order.why: Open with strangers becoming friends in the coffeehouse.
Retain the second version as a distinct recollection.
Consider the remembered time given to visitors.
Turn toward the anguish preceding those encounters.
shortened: What hardship, grief or affliction could be greater than that which occurred at the time when the Blessed Beauty was exiled from Tihran? Hearts of stone were melted. All the relatives were weeping and lamenting. All were in utter despair.

order.why: Read the reported loneliness of the journey.
shortened: For instance, when Baha'u'llah was exiled from Persia with Abdu'l-Baha and the rest of His family, they traveled the long road from Tihran to Baghdad, passing through many towns and villages. During the whole of that journey and distance they did not meet a single believer in the Cause for which they had been banished. At that time very little was known about it in any part of the world. Even in Baghdad there was but one believer who had been taught by Baha'u'llah Himself in Persia. Later on, two or three others appeared.

order.why: Compare the recollection of its thirty stages.
shortened: When they exiled us from Persia, from Teheran, to Baghdad, there are thirty stages -- in these thirty stages we did not find one Bahai. We did not meet one. And now in every one of these stages there are great numbers of Bahai friends.

order.why: Keep the stated route geographically specific.
Attend to the bodily hardship in the winter recollection.
shortened: In Asadabad it was particularly cold. The temperature was 38 degrees below zero. My socks were wet which caused my feet to be frostbitten. That evening we were to eat some halvah. By mistake, however, pepper was added in place of sugar, which severely burned our mouths and throats. That night we did not sleep and constantly drank water. From the blessings of those adversities, those banishments, now the banner of the Divine Faith is hoisted most high!

order.why: Read the reported response within the prime minister’s family.
shortened: At the time of our exile the most noteworthy man, the first man of Persia, was Mirza Aqa Khan, the prime minister.

It was the custom of the prime minister to hold late conferences with the members of his family, and one night, when all were assembled together, his son, who was minister of the treasury, commented most regretfully upon the episode of Baha'u'llah's exile, saying, "What a pity it is that such a noteworthy family should be annihilated because of the acceptance of such a faith!"

order.why: A first-person recollection of accompanying Baha’u’llah in exile to Baghdad as a child.
Hear Baha’u’llah’s account and the rejection of conflict.
shortened: After Our arrival, We revealed, as a copious rain, by the aid of God and His Divine Grace and mercy, Our verses, and sent them to various parts of the world. We exhorted all men, and particularly this people, through Our wise counsels and loving admonitions, and forbade them to engage in sedition, quarrels, disputes and conflict. As a result of this, and by the grace of God, waywardness and folly were changed into piety and understanding, and weapons converted into instruments of peace.

order.why: Preserve the distinct statement concerning official permission.
Read the related explanation without erasing the other accounts of exile.
Consider joy amid poverty on arrival.
Follow Baha’u’llah’s account of solitary withdrawal.
shortened: And when I became aware of his secret and what was in his heart, I departed from Iraq lest there should arise among the servants that which would compromise the dignity of the Cause. We left them to themselves that perchance the fire of negation and wretchedness might be stilled. I wandered through the lands for two successive years, and none knew of My person save God Who created it and fashioned it. Thou knowest that I sent no word or trace of My pen to My family lest they discover the land wherein I dwelt, while they remained in turmoil, trembling and lamentation.

order.why: Read the recollection of return from the mountains.
shortened: Let us meditate over the calamities and hardships of the Blessed Beauty, as well as over His severance and Fortitude, for He was two years in the Kurdish mountains, living solitary and alone in a cave, supplicating all night long. The [Kurds] came around at night and heard His Voice but they knew not who this Person was. Later they discovered who He was. When He came back to Baghdad He had on a very old garment. He had one Kurdish jacket, sleeveless and made of coarse fleece. In this manner he entered our house.

order.why: Turn to renewed teaching and an open door.
shortened: When the Blessed Beauty returned from Kurdistan, only a small band of believers had remained in Persia, and those in Iraq had grown dispirited and had sunk into apathy.

Upon His arrival in Baghdad, however, the Most Great Name flung open the doors and issued a universal summons. The call of God was raised and the fame of His Cause noised abroad. Day and night, the leaders and the learned from amongst all peoples attained His holy presence. The flow of questions and answers was constant, and one and all testified to the sufficiency of His replies.

order.why: Distinguish earlier recognition and partial disclosure.
shortened: The first person who recognized the sublimity and holiness of Baha'u'llah and became certain that He would manifest a momentous Cause was Mulla 'Abdu'l-Karim-i-Qazvini, whom the Bab had named Mirza Ahmad. He was the intermediary between the Bab and Baha'u'llah and was aware of the truth of the matter.

After coming to Baghdad from Persia, Baha'u'llah declared to a certain extent the nature of His mission in the ninth year after the appearance of the Bab, and became known among the friends as the appearance of Husayn. For the people of Persia believed that the appearance of the promised Mahdi must be followed by that of Husayn, that is, of Imam Husayn the martyr, to whom they are indeed most attached and bear the greatest allegiance.

order.why: Read the reported setting of the Hidden Words.
Notice the practice of reciting verses.
shortened: He was among those who were in the presence of the Throne when the Dawning-Place of Revelation was in the land of Iraq, and who would recite the verses of God before the Throne at eventide and at dawn.

order.why: Consider the address to those who witnessed the presence in Iraq.
Enter the small shared room.
Read its joy through the story of a critical guest.
Consider the meal extended to many.
Attend to the remembered gratitude of a poor neighbor.
shortened: I remember when I was a child in Baghdad, there was an elderly man who lived near our house. He was poor, and occasionally we would give him bread. One day I saw him take bread from under his arm - first he would look at each piece of bread, then smile, then thank God, and put it in his mouth. He derived such pleasure from that bread that I have never forgotten it.

order.why: Follow the story of the musician and recognition of talent.
Keep the homely recollection of sleeping on the roof.
shortened: When we were living in Bagdad according to the custom of that country we slept on the roof during the summer months. Always I went up on the roof by nights one month before any one else, did and stayed one month and half longer at the end of the season. The members of the family insisted that I must come down because it was getting cold, but I did not listen to them.

order.why: Consider the fatigue involved in constant hospitality.
Read the recollected discussion of money and motives.
Hear the account of joy despite heat and poverty.
Keep the account of continuing danger in view.
Consider exile retrospectively described as a second breath.
shortened: From Tehran to Baghdad, we did not meet a single believer on the road; in thirty stages of the journey, not one soul. Now it was the departure of the Blessed Beauty that caused the Word of God to be exalted in Baghdad and the fame of God's Cause to be spread abroad.

Had this exile not occurred, this joy and glory would not have been attained. Had He not graced Baghdad with His presence, the Cause would have been obliterated. The blessed presence in Baghdad was a second breath that bestowed new life upon the friends.

order.why: Read the further recollection of unintended growth.
Preserve the concise reported interpretation.
Consider the reported widening of international attention.
Read the account of the period’s expanding influence.
shortened: Eleven years sojourn in Bagdad widened immensely the circle of the influence of the Cause and carried its fame to the four corners of the earth.

order.why: Keep the later interpretation of its far-reaching effects attributed.
shortened: All were in despair, and yet what great wisdom it contained. Were it not for this, the Cause would not have been exalted in Baghdad, the Word of God would not have been upraised, the fame of the Cause would not have reached all regions, the call of God's Cause would not have encompassed the world, these regions would not have been illumined, and the rays of the Sun of Truth would not have reached America. All these were the wisdom of that exile.

order.why: Approach departure and its reported public dignity.
Read the statement about warnings before migration.
Connect departure with the claim of revelation.
shortened: And when the appointed hour of His Revelation struck on this promised Day, the veils of destiny were rent asunder and the divine decree was fulfilled with the departure of the Luminary of the heaven of eternity from the city of Baghdad. This came to pass by reason of what the hands of the malicious had wrought against this Light -- a Light that hath outshone every other in its sacred and wondrous splendour.

order.why: Follow the reported interpretation across subsequent banishments.
shortened: Consider the foolishness of the governments of Iran and the Ottoman Empire in how they banished His Holiness Baha'u'llah from Iran to Baghdad and then to Istanbul, Rumelia, and 'Akka. Their purpose was to obliterate the Cause of Baha'u'llah; yet, they performed the greatest service to His Faith by surrendering the Holy Land to Him, without recognizing it.

order.why: End at the house’s door with the question of absence and remembrance.

questions: What do the coffeehouse, shared room, and meals reveal about how relationships were formed?
How can we read the accounts of permission, banishment, and withdrawal together while preserving their differing emphases?
What distinguishes joy amid deprivation from an argument that deprivation is desirable?
How does Jeremiah’s counsel to exiles compare with the counsels against conflict and the accounts of hospitality?
What do the neighboring subjects of Sulaymaniyyih and the later banishments add to an understanding of renewal in Baghdad?

neighbors.invitation: Read further about withdrawal, solitude, and return.

references.label: 1 · Jeremiah 29:4–7 · Seeking the peace of a place of exile
references.note: Jeremiah addresses those taken to Babylon and counsels them to establish households, cultivate the land, and seek the city’s peace. Compare that responsibility toward a place of displacement with the counsels and encounters recalled in Baghdad. This is a comparison of responses to exile, not an identification of the cities or their historical circumstances.

subjects.displayTitle: The Constitutional Revolution: reform and reconciliation
subjects.introduction: Government and people must blend like milk and honey, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá wrote again and again as Iran’s constitutional revolution unfolded, or the country would be ruined and neighbouring powers would step in. Both sides were counselled; neither listened. A constitutional government that conforms to divine law is preferable to absolute rule, and Bahá’ís promoted its ideals, yet the movement in Tehran fell into factions, clerics used constitutionalism as a pretext for dominion, and in Sirjan, Tabriz and Sangsar believers were killed or driven out while accusations against them shifted with every change of fortune. One instruction urges Bahá’ís to seek election; others forbid any entanglement in disputes that are the playthings of politicians, and each has its own occasion. The Qur’an’s word that true believers conduct their affairs by mutual consultation, set beside prayer and giving, points to the moral habits that make collective life workable [1]. The questions that remain lead into non-participation in partisan politics, the proper relationship between a government and its people, and the past, present and future of Iran itself.
subjects.arc: Begin with reconciliation, examine constitutional ideals and participation, then read the historical conflicts and their costs before returning to education and hope.

order.why: Open with the positive responsibility to reconcile government and people.
Explains nonparticipation in the revolution and urges reconciliation between the government and people of Iran.
Read the explicit preference for constitutional government.
Keep the hope for its legitimate establishment.
Consider the reported gap between constitutional hope and factional practice.
shortened: But when the Persian upraised the banner of Constitution every one became hopeful expecting Persian through the beneficent influence of a democratic government will loom large in the family of the living and progressive nations and will enter upon an arena of upward prosperity and internal development. However instead of uniting all their forces together they formed various political parties with no definite policies save to work against each other and thus heap greater disasters upon the already weakened and disorganized state.

order.why: Read the reported frustration with repeated attempts to form assemblies.
Retain the electoral instruction rather than concealing a tension.
shortened: I wrote to you before that the friends must strive with utmost effort to get some Bahais elected to the National Assembly.

order.why: Read the contrasting refusal of involvement and its stated purpose.
shortened: The purpose of the Baha'is is to raise high the banner of the Most Great Peace and to eliminate the foundation of war and strife from all horizons, to bring all different nations and peoples under the shade of God's unified tabernacle, and to erase racial, national, religious, sectarian and political prejudices from the tablet of the world - so that all regions become one region, all races become one race, and all nations become one nation, until the world of creation finds rest.
Given these lofty aims, how can they sully themselves with these conflicts and disputes which are but the playthings of political figures?

order.why: Consider the circular instruction concerning political affairs.
Read the further direction against entering the disputes.
Identify the positive role of universal reconciliation.
shortened: During the revolution in Iran, praise be to God, you were well-wishers of all and strove for universal peace and reconciliation.

order.why: Return to the recurring image of milk and honey.
shortened: From the beginning of the revolution, it was written repeatedly and both sides were counseled that until government and people mix together like honey and milk, prosperity and success are impossible - Iran will be ruined and finally it will end in the interference of neighboring powers.

order.why: Read the repeated warning about interference from outside.
shortened: You wrote from Iran that it is in disorder. Time and again, in explicit terms in all letters for several years past, it was announced that government and people must mix together like milk and honey, otherwise loss and detriment are certain and established, and ultimately this discord will lead to the intervention of neighboring powers.

order.why: Keep the reported repetition as a separate witness.
Preserve the further reported warning and its source omission.
shortened: At the outset of that revolution in Persia known as the Constitutional Revolution, I wrote again and again that until such time as that government and its people become commingled, even as milk and honey, their success and prosperity will remain entirely unattainable. Persia shall fall into ruin, and the governments of its neighbouring realms will ultimately meddle in its affairs...

order.why: Consider the recollection that counsel to both sides went unheeded.
Read the request to consult earlier letters.
Recognize the speed of upheaval.
shortened: Consider Iran and the constitutional movement, how in so short a span of time they caused so great a storm and convulsion.

order.why: Attend to its effects on agriculture and commerce.
shortened: This revolution affected all conditions and walks of life. There has been no agriculture, no trade and no commerce; nay, rather, in all the provinces there have been political disputes and quarrels between the two parties, namely, the nationalists and the constitutionalists.

order.why: Keep the response to a correspondent’s description situated.
Read the reference to an earlier prediction.
shortened: Thou hast written concerning the upheaval in Iran, this upheaval is explicitly mentioned in the Kitab-i-Aqdas and it is severe.

order.why: Attend to the specific accounts of persecution and accusation.
shortened: However, in Sirjan, the government authorities martyred Jinab-i-Aqa Siyyid Yahya, and in Tabriz, Mirza Hasan, the bloodthirsty mujtahid, became oppressive and issued a decree for the execution of all the friends. Two holy souls were martyred, and if the friends had not dispersed, all would have fallen prey to the sword. Likewise in Sangsar, intense agitation arose, and the oppressors stretched forth the hand of aggression and grievously wronged the friends.

Shaykh Fadlu'llah cried out openly day and night that this oppressed community was the founder of the constitution, and their purpose was to spread their Cause among the people so they might freely publish their Tablets and draw souls to their side.

order.why: Keep the attribution of responsibility within the letter’s historical argument.
Read the reported fear of renewed clerical persecution.
Consider the account of shifting accusations against Baha’is.
shortened: After the revolution occurred, the Yahyais portrayed the Baha'is to the constitutionalists as being from the autocracy party. After the freedom-seekers split into two factions, they portrayed the Baha'is to Sattar Khan as being moderates.

order.why: Read the rejection of blame for the conflict.
Retain the reported criticism of opportunistic allegiances.
Keep the sharp account of motives attributed to this particular movement.
shortened: This constitutional movement in Tehran did not spring from benevolent sentiments nor was it founded on pure intentions. A group of divines, seeking to increase their influence and establish complete dominion over the government and people, used constitutionalism as a pretext. These were the same individuals who would cry out from their pulpits claiming that the Baha'is were enemies of the state.

order.why: Read the condemnation of violence and misleading slogans.
shortened: They mislead and deceive people against the government and into ill-will toward the state. They seek ruin while calling it prosperity; they desire bondage while naming it freedom; they perpetrate oppression and tyranny while speaking of justice; they pursue the misery of the people of Iran while terming it happiness.
In short, the audacity of these ignorant people has reached such a degree that they dared to assault the sacred person of His Majesty and inflicted great cruelty upon the noble form of the King.

order.why: Consider the reported account of hostility toward the Shah.
shortened: At first, when the Parliament was organized, it arose against the Shah, intending to dethrone him. A bomb was thrown at him, and those who committed this act were not captured. The whole of Persia were against him and talked evil of him. In all of the newspapers it was stated that this Shah must be dethroned, that he is not worthy to be a Shah;--to such an extent that he reached the lowest degree of disappointment. The Parliament was wholly against him and in Teheran one hundred and twenty-eight meetings were held against him.

order.why: Read the criticism of upheaval as a means of reform.
shortened: The king, with good intention, desired to establish freedom, but the foolish ones ruined everything, imagining that through sedition and upheaval reform of affairs is possible. Alas, alas! This was the result.

order.why: Consider the argument about clerical political intervention.
shortened: It explicitly states that if religious scholars interfere in political affairs, be assured it will be like the days of Shah Sultan Husayn, the time of Fath-'Ali Shah, and the latter period of Abdul Aziz Khan of the Ottoman Empire. In the first instance Afghanistan devastated Iran, in the second instance half of Iran was lost, in the third instance half the Ottoman territories were squandered and nearly ten million souls perished or were left homeless and forced to migrate.

order.why: Keep the statement about foreign forces in its particular setting.
Retain the surviving fragment of a reported occasion.
Ask what knowledge constitutional practice requires.
Read the reported relation between education and liberty.
Compare the reported expectations surrounding constitutional change in Turkey.
Consider the account of public administration and long-term development.
shortened: Now is the time for all subjects to strive with perfect sincerity, trustworthiness and obedience so that ultimate comfort and ease may be achieved in the center of sovereignty, and the authorities may attend to the administration of internal affairs and external considerations and relationships, and establishing laws for human happiness, and adjusting current dealings, and strengthening legal principles, and increasing national wealth, and promoting scientific benefits, and protecting and ensuring the future.

order.why: Turn toward the expectation of resolving difficulties.
shortened: In these days the regions of Iran are in turmoil, with difficulties arising between the government and people, but these will be resolved.

order.why: Read hope alongside acknowledged further obstacles.
shortened: Thou hadst written about peace and security in the capital of Iran - it will improve and get better in future, though some difficulties lie ahead. However, these will not last.

order.why: Hear the anticipated change from turmoil to renewal.
Read the prospect of stability and justice.
End with hope and prayer for both government and people.

questions: What might the image of milk and honey require from both government and people?
How can approval of constitutional principles coexist with criticism of a particular movement or faction?
What further context would help us understand the differing instructions about participation and elections?
How do the passages and Quran 42:38 connect collective decision-making with moral habits?
What do the accounts of persecution, economic disruption, and foreign intervention reveal about the human costs of political conflict?
What forms of education and reconciliation could give practical substance to hopes for reform?

neighbors.invitation: Examine the distinction between public service and partisan involvement.
Continue the inquiry into mutual responsibilities in public life.

references.label: 1 · Quran 42:38 · Consultation within a life of faith
references.note: The verse places mutual consultation alongside responding to God, prayer, and giving from one’s resources. Compare this moral setting for common affairs with the calls for cooperation and education in the compilation. The verse does not by itself prescribe a modern constitutional arrangement or resolve the historical disagreements represented here.

subjects.displayTitle: Islamic practices: outward forms and living meanings
subjects.introduction: A rosary, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá observes, was meant for repeating the names of God so that the worshipper might come to embody them, generosity, wisdom, self-sacrifice, and it decays into a habit of the fingers when that purpose is forgotten. Every practice of Islam carries the same double possibility. Prayer five times a day, the fast of Ramadán, the pilgrimage and the circling of the Ka‘bih, almsgiving, the sacred nights: the Báb’s own devotional writings honour each of them as having meaning only because God revealed it, and Bahá’u’lláh and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá both explain their symbols and alter some of their laws. Alongside the reverence come sharp criticisms of worship emptied of inward meaning, of a dervish lodge where self-injury passes for ecstasy; such witness belongs to its time and place and is no portrait of a whole community. The Qur’án itself declares that righteousness is not a matter of which way one faces but of faith, generosity, fidelity and endurance [1]. The inquiry widens naturally to Muhammad Himself and to the pilgrimage of Hajj.
subjects.arc: Begin with remembrance becoming character, explore the devotional purposes and forms, then read criticism and changes of law in their particular settings.

order.why: Read the criticism of outward observance without inward meaning.
Open with the purpose of remembrance as embodied qualities.
Recognize the scale of prayer, giving, and fasting.
Consider the divine source of the practices’ significance.
shortened: "O My Creatures! Ye all perform, throughout your lives, with utmost striving and endeavour, my commandments for the sake of attaining My good pleasure. If ye observe the derivative precepts, that is solely because I have revealed them in the Book; if ye recognise the Imams of guidance, or seek My nearness through visiting Their shrines, that is merely because Their names have been alluded to in the Qur'an, if ye acknowledge unto the prophethood of Muhammad, the Apostle of God, blessings of God rest upon Him, that is only because He was My Messenger; if ye circle around Ka'bih, that is merely because I have called it My House, and if ye magnify the Qur'an, that is solely because It is My Word.

order.why: Read the devotional testimony linking creation and recognition.
shortened: Make his eyes, O my God, to be gladdened by there being naught in his knowledge that he would dislike, that all things may bear witness to that for which Thou didst create them - the testimony that there is no God but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God and that the Imams are the Proofs of God and that the Gates of the House are the Manifestations of God's Mystery. For this is that for which Thou hast created, sustained, caused to die and given life to all things.

order.why: Hear the prayer’s reverence for Muhammad and his family.
Read the invocation and praise associated with Ramadan.
Connect fasting with love and remembrance.
shortened: Grant, O my Lord, that the fire of Thy love and the heat produced by the fast enjoined by Thee may inflame them in Thy Cause, and make them to be occupied with Thy praise and with remembrance of Thee.

order.why: Notice the joy of breaking the fast.
Keep the reported description of fasting as a reported statement.
shortened: Now, according to the Mohamadan law a person fasting must not eat or drink anything from sunrise to sunset.

order.why: Identifies prayer and fasting as fundamental laws in the Quranic dispensation and explains their symbolic description.
Read the Bab’s detailed account of obligatory prayers.
Retain the profession concerning religious law in its own setting.
Consider the direction concerning the call to prayer.
Distinguish a longstanding custom from an ordinance.
shortened: During the call to prayer in the Dispensation of the Qur'an, placing the hand beside the ear was an ancient custom and longstanding practice of the muezzins.

order.why: Read the dreamlike account of the call to prayer as reported.
shortened: I seemed to be standing within a great mosque, in the inmost shrine, facing the Qiblih, in the place of the Imam himself.
As I stood I raised loudly the call to prayer.
But it matters not; now that I have uttered the Call to prayer, the vast multitude will of themselves chant the prayer.

order.why: Retain the question without supplying an absent answer.
Keep the brief reported occasion concerning a prayer book.
Read the particular instruction for remembrance and silence.
Follow the Bab’s own account of visiting the holy cities.
shortened: After departing from the city of Mecca, I traveled by land and was honored to reach the pure city of Medina - may God's blessings be upon its inhabitant. Due to my desire to stay in Mecca, I remained in this sacred land and conveyed greetings on behalf of the aforementioned owners in the presence of the Prophet - peace be upon him and his family - and the pure Imams - peace be upon them.

order.why: Consider the festival as an occasion for drawing near to others.
shortened: This is a Day whereon there gather at Thy House, by the word of Thy Beloved, such numbers as none can reckon save Thee, and likewise at His tomb, and similarly before the seat of the One Whom Thou hast mentioned through the words of Thy Beloved. Thus was their remembrance ordained among the servants in Islam, as Thy Beloved made that day a festival wherein they might honor one another, draw close to one another, and approach each other in obedience to Thy Messenger's command and to exalt the Word of Thy Prophet.

order.why: Read the reported explanation of obedience.
Keep the reported symbolic explanation in its source form.
Turn to inward hearing during circumambulation.
Consider the reported argument about the significance of sacred places.
Hear the Aqsa Mosque’s personified praise.
shortened: And from another direction the Aqsa Mosque speaketh forth: "Praise be unto Thee, O God of Names, for I perceive the fragrance of Thy garment from the direction of Thy imprisoned Name."

order.why: Retain the further passage about that sacred edifice.
shortened: God aided him to recognize Him and enabled him to build that renowned edifice which was named the Remote Mosque in the kingdom of creation.

order.why: Read the enumeration of sacred nights as an attributed belief.
Keep the devotional praise of Sha’ban and its stated tradition.
Consider the reported reading of the promised Mahdi.
shortened: In the traditions, the Prophet said to Imam 'Ali: "The Mahdi will come and He will fill the earth with justice, and He is of thy progeny" - this is an allusion.

order.why: Read the remembered encounter with religious scholars.
Attend to the appeal to revealed judgment.
Keep the particular instruction concerning zakat.
Distinguish the Baha’i ordinance concerning congregational obligatory prayer.
Keep the reported scene of inattentiveness particular.
shortened: Mohamadans having forgotten their reverence for the Holy things and overlooking the injunction of Mohamad smoke and talk on such occasions. When I arrived there was a hubbub of confusion, people chatting, smoking, talking and drinking coffee and tea; and in the corner of the room there were two singers who chanted the Koran very beautifully but no one listened to them.

order.why: Read the sweeping reported claim about Ramadan as situated criticism.
Consider the reported dispute over the status of Quranic words.
Read the criticism of a witnessed practice without generalizing it to all Sufis.
shortened: Would that certain souls who claim ardor and attraction, passion and enchantment, and the like, would go to Constantinople and observe the Qadiriyyih monastery and become warned. O Ali! A group is gathered in that place, and by the True One Himself, it hath been witnessed that one of those souls continuously struck himself against stone and mud and wall for more than four hours until there was fear of his perishing. Then he would fall unconscious to the ground and for about two hours would have no awareness at all. And they count these things among spiritual gifts.

order.why: Keep the reported account of veiling historically attributed.
Retain the further criticism without treating it as a universal description.
Consider the polemic concerning attachment to names.
shortened: The heedless ones have clung to names while remaining deprived of their Creator, Source and Lord. Names have become as idols for some, and the Shi'ih sect is truly recorded with God as worshippers of names, and on the Day of Reckoning they have done what no oppressor hath ever done - from pulpits they curse and revile the Object of all the worlds.

order.why: Keep the severe denunciation connected with the account of persecution.
Read the criticism of worship divorced from conduct.
End with the reported reflection on mercy, justice, and the limits of comprehension.
shortened: 'Has the Lord God foreseen that this human being will not let himself be saved, or has He, for reasons inscrutable to us, let him be ensnared from the begin-ning in folly and delusion?' But as the Lord God is not only the Almighty, but also the All-Merciful - for true might and power are always paired with kind-ness and goodness - and is at the same time the Just and the Avenger, we lowly creatures have to bow to His inscrutable decree and believe that the Potter in His absolute wisdom and goodness, in His justice and truth, creates, changes and completes everything to the best for the individual and for the whole -even where our own understanding and comprehension largely fail.

questions: How do the selections connect outward practices with remembrance, recognition, and character?
What does Quran 2:177 contribute to a conversation that includes criticism of empty observance?
How should we distinguish devotional texts, descriptions of custom, reported criticisms, and binding ordinances?
What might the neighboring subject of pilgrimage add that this selection alone cannot show?
How can we examine the loss of meaning in a practice without generalizing about an entire religious community?

references.label: 1 · Quran 2:177 · Worship and the wider demands of righteousness
references.note: The verse refuses to reduce righteousness to the direction one faces. It also affirms prayer and giving, within a wider account of faith, care for vulnerable people, fidelity, and endurance. Compare this integration of practice and character with the selections on remembrance and inward meaning; the passage does not dismiss ritual observance.

subjects.displayTitle: The Declaration of the Bab: recognition and a new dawn
subjects.introduction: A young merchant of Shíráz prepares tea for His guest and, while serving it, recites verses of such beauty that the visitor, a seminary scholar, is astonished; by morning Mullá Ḥusayn has found what he had been searching for. The Báb was twenty-five. He later described the night as an awakening in which the Spirit of God took possession of His soul, and He named Himself the Gate, the channel of grace from One still behind the veil of glory, while also claiming the voice of the Tree of Sinai in the year sixty. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá calls that evening the dawn whose promise was fulfilled in the sunrise of Bahá’u’lláh, and asks that it be celebrated with rejoicing rather than His own birthday. John answering questions about his identity and pointing toward one his hearers did not yet know offers a comparison about preparation and recognition [1], with the difference that the Báb claimed revelation as well as heralding. Birth, banishment and martyrdom belong to the same life, and an anniversary can renew attention to what it commemorates. The way leads on to the station and claims of the Báb and to the events of His ministry.
subjects.arc: Begin with the encounter and the Bab’s own experience, examine the images and claims of a new dawn, then move through sacrifice toward purposeful commemoration.

order.why: Open with the encounter over tea and the recognition of verses.
Hear the Bab’s account of an inward awakening.
shortened: When I awoke, I felt that the Spirit of God had permeated and taken possession of My soul. My heart was thrilled with the joy of His Divine presence, and the mysteries of His Revelation were unfolded before My eyes in all their glory.

order.why: Read the words addressed to the first believer.
Place the proclamation at the stated stage of life.
shortened: As for the Bab---may my soul be His sacrifice!---it was at a young age, that is, in the twenty-fifth year of His blessed life, that He arose to proclaim His Cause.

order.why: Consider the explanation of the title Gate.
shortened: He began to speak and to declare the rank of Bab-hood. Now what He intended by the term Bab [Gate] was this, that He was the channel of grace from some great Person still behind the veil of glory, Who was the possessor of countless and boundless perfections, by Whose will He moved, and to the bond of Whose love He clung.

order.why: Retain the reported account of the Bab’s titles.
Read the strong claim concerning divine manifestation.
shortened: O Baqir! Bear thou witness in thy soul, thy being and thy spirit that the Tree of Sinai hath been raised up in truth in the year sixty and hath spoken in the most exalted voice that there is none other God but Him, the Sovereign, the Powerful, the Almighty, the Mighty, the All-Knowing, and that 'Ali before Nabil - His light, His glory and His sovereignty over the dwellers of the heavens and the earth - hath come with the truth upon clouds of light, and around Him circled the denizens of the Supreme Concourse and the angels drawn nigh.

order.why: Consider the declaration of recognition associated with the year sixty.
shortened: Say: By God! The Spirit at this moment moveth before His presence, and the Sun deriveth its light from His resplendent brow, and the Beauty of the Unseen speaketh above His head with a call that draweth unto it the hearts of those possessed of understanding: "This, verily, is He Who appeared in the year sixty, and this is one of His mighty signs."

order.why: A brief first-person statement connecting Abdu’l-Baha’s birth with the night of the Bab’s declaration.
Preserve the Bab’s numerical and theological language.
Read the festival’s historical description with its uncertain attribution retained.
Introduce the dawn and sunrise comparison.
shortened: This is 23 May, the anniversary of the message and Declaration of the Bab. It is a blessed day and the dawn of manifestation, for the appearance of the Bab was the early light of the true morn, whereas the manifestation of the Blessed Beauty, Baha'u'llah, was the shining forth of the sun. Therefore, it is a blessed day, the inception of the heavenly bounty, the beginning of the divine effulgence. On this day in 1844 the Bab was sent forth heralding and proclaiming the Kingdom of God, announcing the glad tidings of the coming of Baha'u'llah and withstanding the opposition of the whole Persian nation.

order.why: Read the further address on the anniversary.
shortened: "Today is the anniversary of the declaration of the Bab - Peace be upon thee! Today the Bab declared this cause in Shirza, Persia. The appearance of the Bab resembles the dawn, for the dawn holds the promise of the sun. The dawn of the Bab promised the rising of the sun of truth that is to envelop the whole world.

order.why: Consider the particular qualities attributed to dawn.
shortened: This Day is a blessed day, and many Tablets have been revealed for this Day by Baha'u'llah. The Blessed Beauty celebrated this Feast every year. For this Day of the Bab's Declaration is the dawn of the Manifestation of the Cause. The dawn of the day is a very blessed time. Though at dawn the fullness of the Sun's splendor is not manifest, yet as the dawn bears the glad tidings of the rising of the Sun, it is found with exceeding purity and brilliancy and the air is then at its purest.

order.why: Hear Baha’u’llah’s commemoration of the Declaration.
Read the Bab’s address to the promised One.
shortened: And in this second year of my Revelation -- a Revelation which took place at Thy behest -- I bear witness that Thou art the Most Manifest, the Omnipotent, the Ever-Abiding; that of all things that exist on earth and in the heavens nothing whatsoever can frustrate Thy purpose and that Thou art the Knower of all things and the Lord of might and majesty.

order.why: Consider the Primal Point as bearer of glad tidings.
Read the further testimony concerning promise and fulfilment.
Keep the language of manifestation alongside the heralding role.
Read the reported interpretation of the Bab’s first book.
shortened: That which Mirza Abu'l-Fadl stated is proven by the Sacred Text. In the Ahsanu'l-Qisas, which is the first Book of the Bab, He addresses Siyyid Akbar. The Speaker is the Bab, and He says regarding who this Siyyid Akbar is: "By God the True One! I am verily a Houri whom Baha gave birth to in a palace of moist crimson ruby" and "I and those who dwell in Paradise yearn for the soul who is martyred in His path."

order.why: Consider the numerical interpretation of the year nine.
shortened: Then he cites the blessed verse from the Furqan which states "This is but a Reminder for all the worlds, and you shall surely know its tidings after a time," meaning that focal point is the Remembrance of God, and what He announces will become manifest and evident in the year after sixty-eight, which corresponds to the numerical value of "time," and after "time" is sixty-nine, meaning it will bear fruit, just as the Exalted One [the Bab] has stated: "Then in the year nine you shall attain all good."

order.why: Keep the reported prophetic calculation attributed.
shortened: By calculation, the Day of the Bab is foretold, and also the prophecies of the Koran, as to the twelve Imams. One prophecy says that in 1260 A.H. (1844 A.D.) the Day of the Lord shall appear (after the flight of Mohammed).

order.why: Read the additional reported account of expectation.
shortened: After 1260 years this Mehdi or Bab appeared and He said " the morning has dawned and the hour has come. I am this door and have come to prepare the way before Him." The Bab has explicitly declared in the Book of Bayan, that after 19 years the Promised One will appear or come."

order.why: Follow the reported movement from dawn to illumination.
Retain the further dawn and sun imagery.
shortened: At such a time the Dawn of Guidance, His Highness the Supreme, the Bab, appeared, His Holiness Baha'u'llah, like unto a sun, shone forth and all this darkness was converted into light.

order.why: Compare the reported rhythm of religious renewal.
Hear the image of a call awakening divine love.
Return to Shiraz as a place of beginnings.
shortened: O servant of the Self-Sufficient Lord! Shiraz at the beginning of the dawning of the Sun of Truth became a sanctuary of mysteries and the melody and song of the Supreme Concourse began.

order.why: Consider the later spread of life in the Bab’s homeland.
shortened: Praise be to God that in that honored region, which was the native land of His Holiness the Exalted One, may my spirit be a sacrifice for Him, the holy fragrances are spreading and the life-giving breezes from the gardens of bounty are stirring.

order.why: Read banishment as an episode beyond the declaration itself.
shortened: Jesus was forced to leave the Holy Land for Egypt, but this separation became the cause of blessings. Muhammad fled from Mecca to Medina, but His flight resulted in victory. The Bab was likewise banished from Shiraz to the banks of the river Araxes, but auspicious indeed were the results of His banishment!

order.why: Keep the brief recollection of a visitor from Maku.
shortened: He said, "I have come from the fortress of Maku, having attained the honor of meeting His Holiness the Exalted One."

order.why: Follow the later ministry and memories of sacrifice.
shortened: That city was illumined with the presence of His Highness, the Bab, after he left Shiraz; the Word of God was promulgated; many blessed souls became believers; a number of them hastened toward the arena of martyrdom; his highness, the leader of the righteous ones, the "King of the Martyrs," and the master of the friends, the "Beloved of Martyrs," gave up their lives at the altar of love.

order.why: Join the reported heralding role with the sacrifice of life.
shortened: The Bab appeared in Shiraz seventy years ago and gave the glad tidings of the appearance of the Kingdom. He sacrificed His life in the path of God and made souls ready for the love of God.

order.why: Distinguish the lament for martyrdom from the declaration celebration.
shortened: This is the Day when the Sun of Truth was hidden behind the clouds of divine providence. This is the Day when that shining Moon did set. This is the Day when that sacred and delicate Body rolled in dust and blood.

order.why: Read the reported account of Baha’u’llah sustaining the Bab’s Cause.
shortened: If the Blessed Perfection had not exerted Himself to raise up the Cause of God, the Cause of the Primal Point [the Bab] would have been completely effaced.

order.why: Distinguish the birthday commemoration included in the collection.
shortened: This is a Tablet from Our presence to glorify the Night in which heavens and earth were illumined by the Day-Star whose effulgent splendour hath encompassed the dwellers of the whole world.

Immeasurably blessed art thou, inasmuch as the Day of God hath been born in thee -- the Day which hath been singled out by Us to be the lamp of salvation unto the denizens of the cities of names, the chalice of blissfulness for such as dwell within the immensities of the realm of immortality and the source of joy and gladness unto all the inmates of the world of creation.

order.why: Keep the reported festival statement and its supplied date distinct.
shortened: This is the day of the Proclamation of the Bab! It is the Festival of the Forerunner of the Blessed Beauty (Baha'u'llah). It is the day of the dawning of the Morning of Guidance.

order.why: Read the calendar clarification in its original terms.
Consider the instruction to celebrate the Bab’s Declaration.
Enter the account of a feast beside the shrine.
shortened: O joyous Bahhaj!

Yesterday, which was the fifth of Jumada al-Awwal, the Day of the Declaration of His Holiness the Exalted One, they pitched the pavilion near the Holy Shrine and Blessed Tomb (may my spirit be a sacrifice for its dust), and in perfect joy and fragrance the feast of happiness was arranged.

order.why: Read a celebration that also recalls companionship.
shortened: O flowers of the garden of truth! Your letter arrived and its contents made clear that praise be to God, on the Day of the Declaration of His Holiness the First Point, may my soul be sacrificed for Him, you held a heavenly celebration and arranged a divine feast, and recalled those days when 'Abdu'l-Baha met with you in that divine garden and blessed meadow.

order.why: Notice the practices of verses and prayers.
shortened: You wrote about the celebration of the Day of the Declaration of the Bab, that on that day you arranged a feast and engaged in mention of God, recited verses and said prayers.

order.why: Hear the response to an anniversary letter.
shortened: O ye kind friends and the beloved maid servants of His Holiness the Incomparable One!
The letter that you have written on the anniversary day of the declaration of the First Point (the Bab) - may my life be a ransom to him - became the cause of great happiness.

order.why: Read the acknowledgment of celebration at the Mashriqu’l-Adhkar.
Follow the celebration to Paris.
shortened: O divine friends and handmaidens of the Merciful! The congratulations for the Day of the Declaration of the Bab (may my spirit be sacrificed for Him) arrived and I was very pleased that such a grand celebration was held in Paris.

order.why: End with annual remembrance directed toward the glad tidings.

questions: What does the opening encounter suggest about the relationship between expectation and recognition?
How do the images of dawn and sunrise illuminate the relation between the Bab and Baha’u’llah, and what might those images leave unexplained?
How does reading the Bab’s own revelatory language deepen or qualify a comparison with John’s role as a herald?
What distinctions are needed when a compilation includes declaration, birth, martyrdom, and later ministry together?
How could an annual celebration renew understanding and commitment rather than become an exercise in repetition?

neighbors.invitation: Explore the Bab’s claims alongside His role as herald.

references.label: 1 · John 1:19–27 · A herald questioned about his identity
references.note: John answers questions about his identity and directs attention toward one whom his hearers do not yet recognize. Compare the themes of preparation and recognition with the dawn imagery. Preserve a crucial distinction: John denies the proposed titles in this scene, whereas the Bab’s own writings and the neighboring subject express claims to divine revelation as well as a heralding role.
